desc:
Encoding. A non-negative integer is stored as an array of its decimal digits, most significant digit first, one digit per element, with no leading zeros; the number zero is stored as [0]. Results use the same format. The numbers can have thousands of digits, so you cannot convert a whole array into one machine integer.

Compute n! (the product of all integers from 1 to n, with 0! = 1) and return its digits. The result is far beyond any integer type, so you must multiply with arrays.

Example: n = 5 gives [1,2,0]. Example: n = 10 gives [3,6,2,8,8,0,0].
hints: Compute 1 × 2 × 3 × ... one factor at a time and keep the running product as an array of digits.
Multiplying a digit array by a small number m works like multiplication on paper: multiply every digit by m, add the carry from the previous digit, keep the last digit and carry the rest.
Store the digits least significant first so that the array grows at its end. After the digits are used up, append the remaining carry digit by digit. Reverse at the very end.
editorial: Keep the product as a list of digits, least significant digit first. To multiply by m ≤ 600, go through the list: v = digit * m + carry, store v % 10, carry v // 10. When the list ends, flush the remaining carry as new digits (it can be up to three digits long).

Doing this for m = 2..n costs O(n · D) where D is the number of digits of n!, about n log<sub>10</sub> n. For n = 600 that is a few hundred thousand simple steps. Reverse the list at the end to get the most significant digit first.
time: O(n · D) where D = digits of n!
